name: Lemon / tomato juice for dark circles

lead: People dab lemon or tomato juice under the eyes as a home lightener, hoping to fade dark circles. Online communities credit the acidity and vitamin C in lemon and the lycopene and vitamin C in tomato.

The idea is that these ingredients lighten pigment in the thin under-eye skin so circles show less. No published trial has tested either juice on dark circles. Dermatology sources list thin skin, pigment, visible vessels, allergies and sleep loss as causes of dark circles.

paras: Users apply the juice with a cotton pad, often mixed with other ingredients, leave it for several minutes and rinse. It is typically done in the evening, and people describe repeating it over weeks.

Citrus juice on skin followed by sun exposure can cause phytophotodermatitis, a reaction that can leave brown marks lasting months to years. Acidic juice near the eye can sting and irritate thin, sensitive skin, and allergic reactions occur.

web.title: Lemon / tomato juice for dark circles — Grokipedia

angle.text: Online communities apply lemon or tomato juice under the eyes to lighten pigment and reduce the look of dark circles, crediting vitamin C and lycopene. This use on under-eye skin has not been studied, while citrus on sun-exposed skin is known to cause dark marks.

lead: Applying lemon juice or tomato juice under the eyes is a do-it-yourself remedy that online communities say lightens periorbital dark circles. Lemon is acidic and rich in vitamin C, while tomato juice contains lycopene and vitamin C, and proponents credit these for a "lightening" effect.[1]

No published trials were found testing lemon or tomato juice on dark circles. Dermatology sources list thin skin, pigment, vessels, allergies and sleep loss as causes, and report that citrus juice on skin exposed to sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis, a reaction that may leave lasting dark marks.[2][3]

paras: Tomato juice is an unconcentrated beverage of mildly acidic pH, with reported vitamin C and lycopene content.[1] Dark circles have varied causes, including thin skin showing underlying vessels, melanin, allergies and eye rubbing, deficiencies, fatigue and ageing.[2]

Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic reaction that occurs when skin contacts furanocoumarin-containing plants, including citrus, and is then exposed to UV-A light. Reactions peak 48 to 72 hours after exposure and can leave brown or purplish pigmentation lasting years.[3]
Documented treatments for dark circles include topical agents, laser and light procedures, and fillers. Vitamin C-containing eye creams are noted to possibly brighten pigmentation.[2]
No studies found. Studies of tomato lycopene concern dietary intake and blood markers, not topical use on dark circles.[4]
